name: Tomas Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Patel Brothers, which is 350 hectares of potatoes and cereals plus 60,000 free-range laying hens. Mornings start at six in the hen houses with the egg collection belts, then I'm in the potato store checking temperatures, then out on the fields. I use AI tools all day, for planning, for reading the soil sensor data, even for writing the staff rota.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like trying things. We're trialling a robot weeder in the carrots, sorry, the potatoes, my head's in two places, and I run a small drone survey business on the side for neighbouring farms. What wears me out is the hens, honestly. Sixty thousand birds don't care that it's Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool and I'll keep using it. I'd probably post something on the farming forum about the bits that actually work. No point being angry about hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge stays an edge. If most farmers don't bother with AI, the ones who use it well stay ahead. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the tools, keep running the drone surveys, keep pushing the robot weeder trial. I'd probably buy a second drone in the spring, about four thousand. And keep saving, I've got about a year put by plus some shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, like a match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your drone business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine. I've got 14 farms on the books, mostly checking crop health from the air. That carries on. Maybe it grows a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be bored?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I like change. But I'd find something to tinker with, I always do. Last winter it was a sensor in the potato store that texts me if it gets too warm.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a good tool and I'll keep using it. I'd post on the farming forum about the bits that actually work, because there's no point being angry about hype.
S0.think: My edge stays an edge. If most farmers don't bother with AI, the ones who use it well stay ahead, and that's me.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools, runs his drone survey business for 14 farms and continues the robot weeder trial. Buys a second drone in spring for about four thousand and keeps saving.
S0.quote: A tiny bit disappointed, like a match that ends nil-nil.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is the kind of farmer who tinkers for fun. He sees the plateau as protecting his advantage over slower neighbours. His side business gives him income outside the main job and he talks about it casually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when good farm managers earn their keep. I'd be telling other farmers on the forum which robots work and which are rubbish. Practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a great spot. I already know the kit, I already run a side business, and every farm near us would need help setting things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get the robot weeder fully in on the potatoes and look at robotic egg collection in the hen houses. On the side, I'd turn the drone surveys into a small robot setup service for other farms. I'd put maybe ten thousand of my own savings into kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the Patels lean on you to make this happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but they'd trust me to pace it. Raj Patel says I spend his money like it's mine, which from him is a compliment. He only signs off once I've shown him the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads in the hen houses. Three of them, all good workers. If the egg collection goes robotic, I'd need one of them, not three. I'd want to train them on the robots before I'd let anyone go.

S1.say: This is when good farm managers earn their keep. I'd tell other farmers on the forum which robots work and which are rubbish.
S1.think: I'm in a great spot, because I already know the kit and run a side business. Every farm near us would need help setting things up.
S1.do: Fully brings in the robot weeder and looks at robotic egg collection in the first year. Turns his drone surveys into a small robot setup service for other farms, putting about ten thousand of his own savings into kit.
S1.quote: Raj Patel says I spend his money like it's mine, which from him is a compliment.
S1.fieldNote: He moves first and sees the steady picture as an opportunity. His concern for three hen-house workers is real but practical: train them before any cuts. He's willing to put his own money into kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, quickly, and don't pretend it isn't happening. I'd be practical about it: here's what's coming, here's what to do. I'm not one for doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even I don't stay ahead for long. If AI can manage a farm, the Patels need machines and maybe one person. I'd still be better placed than most, but the gap closes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the drone business while it's still worth something, probably to one of the bigger survey firms. I'd put the money and some savings into shares in the companies making farm robots. And I'd automate everything at Patel Brothers I could, so I'm the one running it, not the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like change, but this is a lot of change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your drone business is also something AI could do. What happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It dies, basically. A robot with a camera doesn't need me flying a drone over it. So I'd sell in the first six months, while buyers still think it's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is there anything you'd do right now, this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd ring the bigger survey firm in town this week, just to see what they'd pay. And I'd sit down with Raj Patel and say, let's plan this together, before someone sells him something worse.

S2.say: Get ready quickly and don't pretend it isn't happening. I'd be practical about it, here's what's coming and here's what to do, because I'm not one for doom.
S2.think: Even I don't stay ahead for long, because if AI can manage a farm the owners need machines and maybe one person. I'd still be better placed than most, but the gap closes fast.
S2.do: Sells his drone business within six months, starting by calling a bigger survey firm this week. Invests the money and some savings in farm robot companies and automates as much of the farm as he can so he's the one running it.
S2.feel: Uneasy at how much changes at once, despite liking change.
S2.quote: A robot with a camera doesn't need me flying a drone over it.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptable person here admits his lead vanishes fast in this picture. His response is quick and financial: sell, reinvest, take control of the automation. He stays practical rather than gloomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. Learn the kit, look at what work is left, plan your money. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the best one for me. Long enough to build something, short enough that the slow farms don't catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the drone business and turn it into a robot setup and repair service for the area over the first two years. I'd automate the potatoes and hens at Patel Brothers. And I'd put a bit into robot company shares, but not everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't need to sell in a panic. I could grow the business into robot setup, then sell it at year four when it's worth the most. That's a very different number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who wasn't as prepared as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Gus farms sheep up the valley and won't touch a smartphone. I'd tell him to start saving and let me set his kit up cheap when the time comes. He'd probably tell me where to go.

S3.say: Five years is plenty if you start now. Learn the kit, look at what work is left and plan your money, and that's what I'd tell anyone.
S3.think: Five years is the best one for me, long enough to build something and short enough that the slow farms don't catch up.
S3.do: Turns his drone business into a robot setup and repair service over two years and automates the potatoes and hens at the farm. Puts some savings into robot company shares and plans to sell the business around year four.
S3.quote: Long enough to build something, short enough that the slow farms don't catch up.
S3.fieldNote: He sees the middle timeline as the best for him personally, which is a frank and slightly competitive view. The extra time turns a panic sale into a planned one. He offers to help a less prepared friend, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to get ready, so there's no excuse not to. I'd say learn the tools now, because they're already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is fine, but it lets everyone else catch up. My head start matters less. I'd still be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the robot setup business slowly, maybe take on a partner. I'd do a short course in robotics maintenance in a year or two so I can fix things myself. And I'd buy a few hectares of my own land when prices are right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life with a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at 37. Is that good or bad for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. At 37 I'd be in my best working years with ten years of experience on the new kit. The risk is that I get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stay in farming at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but as the person who runs the machines across several farms, not on one. I'd want a bit of land of my own too. Land doesn't go out of date.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for everyone to get ready, so there's no excuse not to. Learn the tools now, because they're already here.
S4.think: Ten years is fine, but it lets everyone else catch up and my head start matters less. I'd still be all right.
S4.do: Grows his robot setup business slowly, possibly with a partner, and takes a short robotics maintenance course in a year or two. Buys a few hectares of his own land when prices suit.
S4.feel: Calm, like normal life with a project.
S4.quote: Land doesn't go out of date.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually, he finds the long timeline slightly less attractive because it erodes his head start. His plan mixes a tech business with buying land, a hedge between new and old. He names getting comfortable as his own risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because even if I'm fine, most people round here aren't ready. The hen house lads, Gus, my own dad who drives a delivery van. What would help is cheap, quick training on the new kit, run locally, not some online course nobody finishes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people my age see it. We grew up with phones. Most of us aren't scared of the machines, we're scared of the bills. Different thing.

headlineQuote: Most of us aren't scared of the machines, we're scared of the bills.
portrait: Tomas Baker is a 27-year-old farm manager running potatoes, cereals and 60,000 laying hens for a family firm, and he runs a drone survey business on the side. He uses AI tools all day, likes to tinker and sees most of the pictures as chances rather than threats. Only the fast AGI picture makes him uneasy, because his lead closes quickly and his drone business would lose its value, so he'd sell it fast and reinvest. With five or ten years he'd build a robot setup service and buy some land of his own, while worrying more about less-prepared people around him than about himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even if he's fine, most people around him wouldn't be ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick, local training on the new machines, not an online course nobody finishes.
